Intel's FY2024 10-K explicitly stated that the company had "ceased to return capital to stockholders," noting it had not repurchased stock in recent years, had reduced and then suspended its quarterly dividend in the fourth quarter of 2024, and had agreed under its commercial CHIPS Act agreement to forgo paying dividends for the next two years with limitations for the three years thereafter [1]. The FY2025 10-K confirms that no shares were repurchased during the fiscal year ending December 27, 2025, that the last repurchase under the board's authorization occurred in Q1 2021, and that as of December 27, 2025, $7.2 billion remained available under the $110.0 billion authorized repurchase program [2].

On partner co-investments, both the FY2024 and FY2025 filings disclose the same two Semiconductor Co-Investment Program arrangements—the 2022 joint investment with Brookfield in Arizona manufacturing and the 2024 joint investment with Apollo related to Fab 34 in Ireland—and both note the $755 million charge recognized in the fourth quarter of 2024 for penalties related to Ireland SCIP construction delays [3][4]. However, the FY2024 filing frames these arrangements explicitly under a "Smart Capital approach to capital spending," language that the FY2025 filing drops, and the balance sheet shows partner contributions to non-controlling interests surging from $1,702 million in 2024 to $5,108 million in 2025 [4][5].

The most significant structural shift in government funding is disclosed in the FY2025 10-K: during the third quarter of 2025, Intel completed transactions with the U.S. government in which future grant funding under the commercial CHIPS Act agreement and the Secure Enclave agreement was converted into equity investments, with the filing stating the transactions "eliminate our contractual rights to receive future funds under the commercial CHIPS Act agreement and Secure Enclave agreement in the form of grants [6]." The FY2025 filing also introduces the concept of "Escrowed Shares"—shares of Intel common stock held in escrow to be released to the U.S. Department of Commerce as Intel performs and receives cash proceeds under its CHIPS Act Secure Enclave agreement, with any unreleased shares at the end of the performance period split between forfeiture and transfer to the DOC at no consideration [7]. By contrast, the FY2024 10-K described a November 2024 direct funding agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce under the CHIPS Act that included detailed milestones for receiving grants, restrictions on certain change-of-control transactions, a requirement to share project returns above specified thresholds with the U.S. government, and termination rights allowing for potential repayment of some or all awards [8].

The FY2025 10-K adds an entirely new category of risk around the U.S. government becoming one of Intel's largest stockholders, warning that the equity issuances are dilutive to existing stockholders, that the U.S. government's equity position reduces the voting and other governance rights of other stockholders, and that the transactions may limit Intel's ability to pursue strategic transactions beneficial to stockholders [9]. The filing further cautions that it is uncertain whether the transactions may cause other government entities to seek to convert their existing grant arrangements with Intel into equity investments or be unwilling to support Intel with future grants, either of which could limit Intel's access to capital [9].
